passages.t: Three weeks of mourning, and a man dressed in linen
passages.happening:
‘In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, a message was revealed to Daniel’ (verse 1). The message was true, and it concerned a great conflict.

Daniel had been mourning for three full weeks. ‘I ate no rich food, no meat or wine entered my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil until the three weeks were completed’ (verse 3).

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month he is standing on the bank of the great river, the Tigris (verse 4). He looks up and sees ‘a certain man dressed in linen, with a belt of fine gold from Uphaz around his waist’ (verse 5). His body is like beryl, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his arms and legs like polished bronze, ‘and his voice like the sound of a multitude’ (verse 6).

The men with Daniel do not see the vision, but terror falls on them and they run and hide (verse 7). Daniel is left alone. His strength drains away and his face goes deathly pale (verse 8). As he listens to the man's voice, he falls into a deep sleep with his face to the ground (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 10 to 12 are one final vision, the longest in the book, and this chapter is its prologue. The third year of Cyrus is about 536 BC, the latest date in the book. Daniel would have been in his eighties.

The exiles had been free to go home for about two years, and some had gone. But the news from Jerusalem was not good. The returned community was small and poor, and opposition had stalled the rebuilding of the temple. Daniel is mourning. The first month is Nisan, in spring, so his fast ran through Passover, the feast of the exodus. He spent the festival of freedom in grief, perhaps over the slow and struggling return.

The man in linen is described in terms drawn from Israel's worship and from Ezekiel's visions. Linen was the garment of priests, and of the heavenly scribe in Ezekiel. His dazzling appearance recalls Ezekiel's vision of the glory of God. The Hebrew calls the Tigris by its ancient name, Hiddekel, the name used for one of the rivers of Eden.

The chapter is built around Daniel's weakness. He sees, and loses all strength. What follows is a series of touches that restore him.
passages.later: Ezra records why the rebuilding stalled: ‘the construction of the house of God in Jerusalem ceased, and it remained at a standstill until the second year of the reign of Darius’ (Ezra 4:24). And Revelation describes the risen Christ in words close to these: ‘His feet were like polished bronze refined in a furnace, and His voice was like the roar of many waters’ (Revelation 1:15).
passages.asks: Daniel mourned through the feast of freedom, because the freedom had not turned out as he hoped. Ask what promised good in your life has come more slowly or more poorly than you expected. And ask whether you can bring that disappointment to God as honestly as Daniel did.

passages.t: Highly precious, and a delay in heaven
passages.happening:
A hand touches Daniel and sets him trembling on his hands and knees (verse 10). The messenger says, ‘Daniel, you are a man who is highly precious. Consider carefully the words that I am about to say to you’ (verse 11). Daniel stands up, trembling.

The messenger tells him not to be afraid, ‘for from the first day that you purposed to understand and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come in response to them’ (verse 12).

‘However, the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days. Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me’ (verse 13). Now he has come to explain ‘what will happen to your people in the latter days’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Daniel's prayer was heard on the first day. The answer took three weeks to arrive, and the messenger says why: he was opposed by the prince of the kingdom of Persia for twenty-one days, until Michael came to help.

Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take these princes as spiritual beings, not human rulers, because they fight alongside and against angels. The idea that nations have heavenly princes over them is found elsewhere in the Old Testament, where God divides the nations and sets their boundaries according to heavenly beings, and in Psalm 82. Michael, whose name means who is like God, is here the prince of Israel.

The first hearers were told that their history had an unseen side. The conflicts of empires that chapter 11 will describe are shown to have a spiritual dimension, and God's people have a champion in them.
passages.later: Michael appears again at the end of this vision as ‘the great prince who stands watch over your people’ (Daniel 12:1). The New Testament names him too: in Revelation ‘Michael and his angels fought against the dragon’ (Revelation 12:7), and Jude calls him ‘the archangel Michael’ (Jude 1:9).
passages.hard:
Are there spiritual princes over nations, and could an angel be delayed?

The chapter speaks plainly of a prince of Persia who resisted God's messenger for twenty-one days, of a prince of Greece still to come, and of Michael as Israel's prince. Most interpreters take these as spiritual beings, which fits other passages that speak of heavenly beings associated with the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 82).

Readers differ on how far to press the details. Some take the chapter as a literal description of spirits over territories and draw lessons for prayer and spiritual warfare. Others caution that apocalyptic writing uses vivid pictures to reveal the spiritual meaning of historical events, and that the text says nothing about how people should identify or engage such powers. These notes take no side between them.

What the chapter clearly teaches is that history has an unseen dimension, that God's purposes meet real resistance, and that the resistance does not prevail. The messenger comes. It gives no one a warrant to name any nation or people of the present day as ruled by an evil prince.
passages.asks: Daniel's words were heard on the first day, and the answer took three weeks. Ask how you read delay in your own prayers. And ask whether you could believe, in a long wait, that you are highly precious to God.

passages.happening:
Daniel sets his face to the ground and cannot speak (verse 15). Then one like a man touches his lips, and he says, ‘My lord, because of the vision, I am overcome with anguish, and I have no strength’ (verse 16). How can a servant speak with such a lord, when no breath is left in him (verse 17)?

Again the one like a man touches him and strengthens him (verse 18). “Do not be afraid, you who are highly precious,” he says. “Peace be with you! Be strong now; be very strong!” (verse 19). And Daniel is strengthened and says, ‘Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me’ (verse 19).

The messenger says he must return to fight the prince of Persia, and after that the prince of Greece will come (verse 20). ‘But first I will tell you what is inscribed in the Book of Truth’ (verse 21). No one stands with him against these except Michael, Daniel's prince.
passages.hearers:
Three touches restore Daniel. A hand sets him on his hands and knees. A touch on his lips lets him speak. A final touch strengthens him to hear. Twice he is told he is highly precious, and twice not to be afraid.

The narrative slows on purpose, building toward the revelation that begins in chapter 11. The messenger's words frame what follows: the conflict with Persia and then Greece in heaven matches the earthly history of Persia and Greece in the next chapter. Chapters 10 to 12 should be read as one unit. The chapter breaks were added later and cut the vision into pieces.

The prince of Greece points ahead to Alexander the Great, who conquered the Persian Empire in the 330s BC. Those who date the book to the second century BC read the chapter as the introduction to a survey of history written from the time of Antiochus IV. Those who hold the traditional date read it as true foresight given to Daniel in the Persian period.

The Book of Truth is the record of what God has decreed. The first hearers were being told that what would come was written already, and that God's people were not left without a defender.
passages.later: God spoke the same words to Gideon: ‘Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die’ (Judges 6:23). And to Joshua: ‘Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go’ (Joshua 1:9).
passages.asks: Daniel could not speak until he was touched, and could not hear until he was strengthened. Ask where you need God to strengthen you before you can even listen. And ask who in your life needs you to say what the messenger said: do not be afraid, peace be with you.
